messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber was 37 when he came to treatment, a divorced financial analyst who had spent months trying to keep his life arranged into spreadsheets and routines after a period of captivity that, in his own mind, remained far more immediate than anything else in his past. He described being held against his will in a confined place where he was controlled by others and cut off from any ordinary sense of choice. What stayed with him most was not only the fear, but the humiliating way he had been handled and spoken to. He remembered long stretches in which he was forced to wait in near total silence, listening for movement and trying to guess what would happen next. At other times he heard children crying somewhere nearby, thin and intermittent, and those sounds became fused with his fear and helplessness. He could still recall the smell of the place with disturbing precision, and when he spoke about it in session he would sometimes stop mid-sentence, as if the odor had returned to the room around him.

Daniel did not describe the event in a distant, narrative way. The memories arrived with an intensity that made ordinary recollection seem flat by comparison. He said the images were exceptionally clear, "too clear," with details he wished he could lose. When they came up, they felt more real than normal memories, almost like being dropped back into the same space rather than thinking about something that had happened before. The smell was especially unsettling because it seemed to bypass thought altogether. He could be sitting in an office conference room or in his apartment kitchen and suddenly have the unmistakable sense of that captive space around him.

In the months afterward, certain moments began to stand out as hard to tolerate. Children crying was one of the strongest. On paper Daniel worked in finance, but much of his day involved commuting through busy public spaces and sharing an office building with families in the lobby and on the sidewalk outside. If a child started crying in the elevator bank or on the street below his office, his body reacted before he could reason with himself. He would go rigid and scan the area, his mind fixed on the old feeling that distress was nearby and that something terrible might follow. Silence was just as difficult, though in a different way. Sudden complete quiet in his apartment at night was unbearable because it resembled the suspended waiting he had known in captivity. He found himself staying awake, listening for sounds in the building, convinced he needed to remain alert. Falling asleep felt like giving up watch. Even at home he did not experience himself as safe; he checked locks repeatedly, listened for changes in the hallway, and kept himself poised as if interruption could come at any moment.

Physical affection also became fraught. Since his divorce he had been living alone, but he still had family and a small number of friends who tried to comfort him in ordinary ways. A hand on his shoulder or an offered hug made him tense and pull back. He struggled to explain this without sounding cold. What others experienced as warmth, he experienced as the beginning of being handled, positioned, or controlled. The recoil embarrassed him and gradually narrowed his social world. He skipped family gatherings where greetings were physical and began keeping conversations brief enough that no one would move closer.

As he tried to make sense of himself, Daniel had come to believe that the captivity had done more than frighten him. He spoke with shame about having acted in ways that went against who he believed himself to be. He did not elaborate dramatically, but the meaning was clear: under coercion, he had complied, pleaded, and behaved in ways that felt incompatible with the competent, self-controlled man he had taken himself to be. Alongside this was a more corrosive sense that during the ordeal he had not been treated as a person at all. He used language of being used, moved, and reduced, as if his wishes and identity had been irrelevant. What embittered him further was his conviction that the people responsible had faced no consequences. He followed developments obsessively and found himself stuck on the fact that there had been no real accountability. To him this was not abstract injustice; it meant the world was still arranged in a way that left him exposed.

By the time he sought help, the strain was showing at work. He was still performing, but with effort, sleeping poorly because he stayed vigilant into the night and arriving already exhausted. He avoided informal office contact and left quickly at the end of the day to limit unpredictable encounters. The final push came after he froze in the lobby when a child began crying and a colleague, trying to reassure him, stepped in for a brief hug. Daniel jerked away sharply enough to draw attention, then spent the rest of the day shaken and ashamed. When he came in, what frightened him most was the sense that his own home, his own body, and even ordinary human closeness no longer felt reliably his. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget what happened, but for the memories to stop arriving with such force and for everyday life to stop feeling like a place where he had to stay on guard.
